question.problem: Which root(s) of the polynomial $P(x)=(x+3)({x}^{2}-4)^{3}$ have multiplicity $3?$
question.worked_solution:
The multiplicity of a root of a polynomial equals the exponent of its corresponding factor in the factorization of the polynomial.

First, let's factor $P(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x) & =(x+3)({x}^{2}-4)^{3} \\  & =(x+3)((x+2)(x-2))^{3} \\  & =(x+3)(x+2)^{3}(x-2)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:

- The factor $(x+3)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $P(x).$ So the root $x=-3$ has multiplicity $1.$

- The factor $(x+2)$ has an exponent of $3$ in the factored form of $P(x).$ So the root $x=-2$ has multiplicity $3.$

- The factor $(x-2)$ has an exponent of $3$ in the factored form of $P(x).$ So the root $x=2$ has multiplicity $3.$

Therefore, the roots with multiplicity $3$ are $x=-2$ and $x=2.$
